coherence.reasons: Both run the same sound chain: bridge, why the draft plan fails, sized levers, sequencing, covenant, decisions. X is tighter. Its governing thought, six levers, waves and board asks stay aligned, and its calendar is consistent: it treats FY2026 as closing just before the February 2027 board, so it tests the covenant on run-rate and sets the three-store gate at Q3 FY2027. Its one slip is one-time cost: $18M on the resources slide, but the wave table and store slide imply about $19.5M because the $1.5M closure cost for the three stores is left out. Y has more seams. It dates the deck February 2027 yet builds an FY2026 in-year capture bridge and schedules a vote for 'Q3 FY2026', which only its appendix caveat reconciles. The governing thought says 'rather than cutting labor' while the plan relies on a 3% net hours reduction. The self-set 'initial hypothesis' slide sits awkwardly in the summary, and it switches between six and nine levers and between 80% and 87%. Y's arithmetic and wave totals do reconcile internally.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the key's preferred recommendation (R1 with a targeted labor element): reprice delivery, prune losing promotions, cut shrink, schedule labor to demand, grow private label, exit six stores at lease end and gate the three long-lease stores behind a board vote. Y weighs alternatives more fully. It has a four-option table including 'defend on price' and 'exit home delivery' (sized at up to +$6M and held as a fallback because of the owners' commitment). It separates six data-backed levers (2.5%) from three negotiated ones (3.0%), so the board sees which part of the target depends on vendors and a vote. It gives a break-even on promotion volume loss (41%), a break-even delivery fee ($15.44), and the cost of waiting on the three stores (~$1.1M against $7.5M). X's trade-off handling is good but thinner: blanket versus targeted labor, the '$7.6M visible cost' of keeping delivery, and fix-or-exit for the three stores. X's covenant judgment is the more realistic one: FY2026 is largely set, so brief the lender and seek a waiver if needed. Y's Wave 1 is optimistic, crediting the full promotion lever and a negotiated contract gain as 'proven'.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key's numbers: margin 3.37% to 1.02%, driver ranking with labor at about 13%, e-commerce drag of $10.4M, the 6.1% rebuttal, store closure gain of $6.6M and a target near $42M. Both rebut the category team's comps claim the same way. Y uses the evidence more deeply. It decomposes labor into a wage effect (+1.11 pts) and a productivity effect (−0.77 pts), rebuilds the fulfillment line from Table 5 for all three years, gives the shrink risk as a half-to-full range ($5–10M) and adds sensitivity tables. But Y overclaims in places. 'Deeper promotions did not protect' the ValuMart stores has no counterfactual. 'Cutting less than half of the money-losing events' mixes share of sales with share of events. Its FY2026 bridge rests on capture rates and two mid-year closures that are impossible if the board meets in February 2027, and its 2.2% shrink target is below the best quartile. X is more restrained: it labels the shrink link an association, values lost delivery sales more precisely (30% new × 20¢), and declines to claim FY2026 in-year gains. X's weaknesses are a point estimate for shrink give-back, a private-label pace above trend, and the roughly $1.5M one-time cost inconsistency. Y's deeper use of evidence and X's fewer overclaims roughly offset.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise the CFO/COO view. Both show labor is about 13% of the fall, that wages rose 9.4% but hours per $1,000 fell 6%, that the 8% cut risks shrink, and that freezing e-commerce locks in a roughly $10M loss. Both run the draft plan forward to roughly 1–1.5% margin in FY2028. Y handles the hypothesis slightly more precisely. It quantifies what is right in management's view: wage inflation is real, productivity has already absorbed about $12M, and the 2027 step adds about $7M that needs a targeted labor response. It links past hours reductions to the shrink rise, keeps the useful part of the draft ('freeze for home delivery only'), and tests the draft against both the covenant and the 3% target under low and high shrink. It also tests and revises its own counter-hypothesis, showing that commercial fixes alone reach only 1.8%, which guards against over-correcting. X's draft-versus-recommended comparison is clear and fair, but it simply drops the freeze and gives less credit to what the wage view gets right.

overall.reasons: The two documents are close: same diagnosis, near-identical lever set and sizing, both adding up to about 3.0% within the $25M cap, with second-order effects acknowledged. Y gives the CEO somewhat more to decide with. It compares options explicitly, separates data-backed levers (2.5%) from negotiated ones (3.0%), quantifies sensitivities and a combined downside (2.32%), gives break-evens for promotions and delivery, and tests the management plan against both covenant and target. X is tighter and more honest about the calendar: FY2026 is effectively closed by the February 2027 board, so it proposes a lender briefing rather than in-year capture. Y's FY2026 bridge and 'Q3 FY2026' vote sit uneasily with a February 2027 board, though Y flags this in its appendix. On balance Y's fuller weighing of alternatives and risks outweighs X's cleaner consistency, but only narrowly.
